world.bio: I own a small independent pharmacy in the Annex neighbourhood of Toronto. I have been a pharmacist for twenty-two years and bought this shop eleven years ago. I know half my regulars by their dogs' names. We do blister packs, vaccines, compounding on a small scale, and MedsCheck reviews. I like conversations at the counter more than I like paperwork, though the paperwork is most of the job.
skills_assets: Licensed pharmacist (Ontario College of Pharmacists), certified to give injections
Independent pharmacy with a consultation room, two technicians and a part-time delivery driver
Provides free government-funded MedsCheck medication reviews for seniors on three or more medications
Blister packaging service for a nearby retirement residence
Relationships with local family doctors and a visiting nurse program
Experience supervising pharmacy students during placements

projects.name: MedsCheck outreach
projects.text: I run MedsCheck reviews, funded by the province, for seniors who take three or more medications. This year alone I have caught four cases where a patient was taking two blood-pressure drugs from different prescribers that doubled up, and the dizziness was the result. I would like to get more seniors in the door but the system relies on word of mouth and I have no time for outreach.

projects.name: Back-room renovation
projects.text: Renovating the storage room behind the dispensary into a quiet consultation space. The contractor is two weeks behind. Meanwhile boxes of stock are stacked on the sidewalk side of the shop.

notes.text: Half-marathon training: 10 km this morning along the lake. Knees are fine. Realized I am happier running than I am at the counter on a Monday. Make of that what you will.

Mrs. Okonkwo came in with her bag of pills, again. I do love these sessions. She says the little white one makes her dizzy. Found out she was getting two prescriptions for the same thing. Called the doctor. Dizziness explained. That is the fourth one this year. It reminds me why I do this.
Son's university applications. He wants engineering. I wanted him to see the world of health sciences. He rolled his eyes. I shut up and made dinner.
The contractor says the back room will be ready end of October. I do not believe him. The dust is on everything including the Aspirin.

My last student assistant graduated in August. I have kept her paid, flexible position open. Several applications came in but I do not want someone who will leave in three months. I want a health-sciences student who will stay, whom I can teach properly. It is slow and the counter is chaotic without help.

Husband says I should hire a normal pharmacy tech and stop being picky. I know he is right. But the tech route is a different thing. A student who is interested in the profession asks better questions.
Blister pack error caught at the last minute. A tired tech put the wrong pill in Tuesday evening. No harm. I called a staff meeting. Everybody apologized. I realized I have been tired for weeks.
Dog-walking customer asked about her Labrador's arthritis meds. I said I only do people. She laughed and said everybody in this neighbourhood needs a pharmacist for their dog too.

messages.text: David: Dinner at 7? Me: I will be late, MedsCheck at 5:30. David: Another one? Me: This one has nine medications. David: I'll keep it warm.
Contractor: Delay on the drywall. Me: How long? Contractor: About ten days. Me: You said that last week. Contractor: Supply issue. Me: I need the room by the end of the month.
Ethan: Mom, can you proofread my personal statement? Me: Of course. Ethan: Do not rewrite it. Me: I promise. Ethan: You always rewrite it. Me: Just the commas.
Dr. Patel: Thanks for catching the duplicate on Mrs. Okonkwo. Me: Happy to. Dr. Patel: Send me the others. Me: I will.
Sandra: Do we have a student coming? Me: Not yet. Sandra: We are a bit swamped. Me: I know. I will find someone good.
